lines.note: The opening lhas continues the preceding page's Portuguese word. Zashiki wo uchiharau means sweeping or clearing the room; the translation begins Var and continues as rer on the next physical row, without supplying a terminal hyphen.

Completes varrer and says to clean the zashiki. The room-name Zaxiqui is embedded within the Portuguese explanation and is upright in the print; Tçuyuuo begins the next Japanese example, with dew as its object.

Tsuyu wo uchiharoute tooru means passing along while shaking off the dew. The historical -oute form and the printed separation vchi farǒte are preserved; the Portuguese supplies the same motion and action.
The dew is specifically that on the path. This short Portuguese continuation completes the previous example and does not introduce another headword.
Uchihare describes a place becoming clear or open. The Portuguese deſa- continues into bafado below; its physical division is retained.
Completes desabafado, open or unobstructed, and adds uncovered. The scan has f in bafado and h in Vchi; Vchi fareta begins the example of an open place.
Tokoro completes uchi hareta tokoro, a clear, exposed place. Lugar deſabafado and eſcampado describe the same setting; enlargement corrects the OCR's extra i and broken word boundary.

Ame ga uchi hareta describes the rain clearing. The printed paragraph sign is restored before the example, and vchi corrects OCR vcni; Portuguese Estear a chuua introduces the clearing-weather translation.
Ficar o tempo sereno completes the weather example: the weather becomes clear. The visible fi sequence restores ficar from OCR fcar, without modernizing the rest of the phrase.
Uchihatashi, uchihatasu, uchihataita means killing or bringing something to an end. The aita principal part preserves the historical s-verb inflection instead of imposing modern -shita.
De todo completes acabar de todo, finishing completely. The initial t is visible; OCR lodo would give an unrelated noun and does not fit the type or the construction.
Uchihishigi and its principal forms denote breaking or crushing. The Portuguese begins a synonymous phrase, fazer em pedaços, across the physical line break.
Pedaços completes fazer em pedaços, making into pieces. The cedilla and short continuation are preserved independently of the following entry.

Uchihouke means becoming dazed or foolish, here in absorption in gambling. The headword's worn accent has the rising right arm of a caron; Vchifǒqe is chosen, supported by the clearer example fǒquru below and the supplied NINJAL lexical checkpoint, while the headword mark remains less distinct.
The gloss describes seeming stupefied, especially while playing. The historical printed jugando is preserved, and the sentence continues with absorption in the game on the next row.
Embebido no jogo specifies being engrossed in play. Bakuchi ni uchi- begins the example of becoming absorbed in gambling; the printed line-end hyphen belongs to this divided verb.
Fǒquru completes the preceding vchi- to form uchihoukuru. This short Japanese continuation supplies the inflected example and has a clear caron over o.
Uchihoroboshi means destroying through killing. The principal forms and the Portuguese destruction gloss are retained; the manner is further specified on the following line.
Ou cortando adds cutting as the other destructive action. It completes the same entry rather than supplying a separate verb headword.
Uchifuri denotes brandishing or swinging a weapon. The Portuguese lists sword and staff, with bor- continuing into dão on the next physical row.
Bordão and vara complete the weapon examples. Te, alternatively mi, supplies hand or body as the object of uchi-furu; Latin l introduces the alternative, not part of a Japanese word.

runs.text: Bulir, & menear as maos, ou o corpo.

lines.note: Furu completes the Japanese example. The translation explains moving or shaking the hands or body; printed maos is retained without supplying an absent tilde.
Uchifuse is knocking someone down by striking. Dando em alguem begins that causal action, and der- continues into ruballo below.
Ruballo completes derruballo, to knock him down. The doubled l and separate physical continuation are preserved.
Uchifushi is referred to Fuxi, ſu, the base verb concerning lying or falling down. Vide is the Portuguese/Latin reference instruction; the upright referenced form is kept in the transcription.
Uchiganawa is defined as a trivet made from beaten iron. The short material description supports the utensil sense without adding construction details absent from the source.

Uchigatana is a long sword compared with a montante. Catana appears within the Portuguese explanation and is marked for typeface review; the abbreviation tilde in montãte is preserved without imposing a modern sword classification.

runs.text: Hũa bolſa larga, ou caixa hum pou

lines.note: This uchigaye is a large pouch or a somewhat curved box. The final pou continues into co; no hyphen is supplied where the scan does not clearly print one.

runs.text: co arcada, que ſe leua na cinta com algum co-

lines.note: The container is carried at the waist and contains food. The scan supports cinta, not OCR cunta; co- begins comer on the following row.
Mer completes comer, meaning food here. Dentro closes the description of food carried in the waist container.

runs.text: O que ſe dà em troco de outra couſa

lines.note: The separate uchigaye entry means something given in exchange for something else. Its independent definition is retained despite the identical preceding headword.
The exchange sense is used especially of fields or land. X. is an upright regional label; the punctuation is kept with that label rather than italicized as part of the gloss.
Uchigaye bukuro is equated with uchigaye. The Portuguese begins the description of a pouch or bag, and the synonym after i is not treated as an embedded Portuguese term for typeface marking.

runs.text: ſaco onde ſe mete aquela caixa, ou boceta com

lines.note: The bag holds the previously described box or small container. This is a continuation of the carrying-bag definition and retains the historical demonstrative aquela.

runs.text: comer dentro como fazem os ſoldados, ou os

lines.note: Food is carried inside it as soldiers do. The scan supports ſoldados, correcting OCR foldatos; the explanation extends to travellers on the following line.
Que caminhão completes the reference to those who travel. It is the second group using the food container, alongside soldiers.
Uchigomi describes people or horses moving in a disorderly group. The Portuguese sentence continues to specify the lack of order.
Sem ordem supplies that lack of order. Uchigomi no ikusa then illustrates an army or body of troops advancing without a regular formation.

runs.text: ou gẽte de guerra que vai, ou acomete ſem or-

lines.note: The troops go or attack without order. The divided or- belongs to ordem below, and gẽte retains its printed abbreviation tilde.
Dem completes ordem, then uchigomi ni noru illustrates riding in this disorderly manner. Cavalgar begins the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: ou ir a caualo ſem ordem.

lines.note: Ou ir a cavalo sem ordem completes the riding example. This is an alternative wording of the same unorganized movement.
Uchigiri ni iru introduces an archery action. The Portuguese explains shooting an arrow, with the abbreviated cõ for com retained.

runs.text: ſeta ſem virar o arco na mão de maneira q̃ fi-

lines.note: The archer shoots without turning the bow in the hand. The following clause describes the position of the string; the printed q̃ and fi- are preserved.
Que completes fique and describes the bowstring facing forward. Yugayexi is a separate upright Japanese example within the entry, not italic Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Virar o arco deſta maneira de pois de atirar.

lines.note: Yugaeshi is explained as turning the bow in this way after shooting. The printed spacing de pois is preserved instead of normalized to depois.

Uchigumori is described as Torinoco paper with a wavy or variegated appearance. The initial vowel in Torinoco and the e in ondeado are abraded; the surviving shapes and paper context support these chosen readings over garbled OCR. Torinoco is an embedded Japanese paper name printed in italic, unlike the upright Naguinata elsewhere on this page.
Completes como jaspeado: marbled or jasper-like in various colours. Enlargement supports the initial j of jaſpeado and final s of varias, absent from the OCR.
Uchiguri denotes chestnuts pounded and crushed. Piladas is visible in the scan, correcting OCR plladas; the historical Castanhas spelling and its provisional st classification are retained.
Uchigushi, uchigusuru, uchigushita means taking someone along. The Portuguese leuar consigo supplies the accompanying sense directly.
Uchiidashi means taking or bringing something out. The two adjacent i stems in Vchiidaxi were joined by the OCR as u; the scan and the following example support the doubled vowel.
Vide Vchidaſu refers to the related verb. Ninjuu wo uchiidasu illustrates sending people out, and its purpose is explained on the next row.
The people are sent out to fight. This completes the military use of uchiidasu rather than adding another headword.

runs.text: O morrer na guerra pelejando. Vt,

lines.note: Uchijini is dying in battle while fighting. Vt introduces the verbal example on the next row.
Uchijini suru makes the noun into the expression for dying in battle. It is a complete short example and remains a separate physical line.
Uchiire is making troops withdraw or bringing them back. The headword uses printed j in Vchijre; it is not normalized to the i spelling of neighbouring forms.
Ninjuu wo uchi iruru means bringing the troops in. The printed space within vchi iru- and the line-end division are retained.
Ru completes iruru and Idem refers to the preceding military meaning. Inu wo uchiiruru introduces a different example involving training a dog by punishment; Cas- begins its Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: tigando o cão cuſtumalo a não comer o falcão.

lines.note: The dog is trained not to eat or attack the falcon. The source explicitly uses comer; the transcription does not replace it with a modern falconry expression.
Uchiireta inu is the trained dog. The paragraph sign and second i are visible and restored; its gloss continues with the prohibition on eating the falcon.
Mer completes comer and closes the trained-dog example. The repeated falcon reference links this continuation to the preceding two examples.
Uchiiri, uchiiru, uchiitta is the intransitive counterpart: the troops withdraw or retire. The headword Vchiiri corrects the OCR's unconverted Vcnuiri.
Gente de guerra supplies the subject of the withdrawal. The short continuation belongs to the same troop-movement entry.
Uchimagire first means being very occupied or absorbed. The next paragraph gives the related sense of becoming mixed in.
The second gloss is mixing in. Teki ga mikata- begins the example of enemies mingling with one's own side, continued below.
Ni uchimagireta completes the example of intermingling. The Portuguese Miſturarãoſe has the visible nasal ending and reflexive ſe, while hũa corrects OCR bũa; the people of one side are the subject.

runs.text: parte na guerra com os inimigos.

lines.note: Completes the statement that one side mixed with its enemies in war. This clarifies that the preceding example concerns opposing forces becoming intermingled.
Uchimajiri means mixing with something or being mixed among it. The printed principal part itta is retained, without substituting a modernized morphological spelling.
Couſa completes algũa couſa, followed by the alternative ir de miſtura. Both Portuguese expressions explain the mixing sense of uchimajiri.
Uchimame denotes pounded or crushed beans. The tilde is printed over e in Feijoẽs; it is not moved to o to match modern feijões.
Uchimaqe means suffering defeat. The apparent OCR space after Vchi falls in an abraded part of the m; the headword is read continuously, and Ficar is recovered from its damaged c.
The defeat may be in war or in a game. This short gloss continuation provides both contexts for uchimake.
Uchimaqi is a women's-register term for rice. The source's sociolinguistic label is reported as printed, without inferring the exact modern rice category.
Uchimata is the opening or root of the legs, the inner-thigh or crotch area. The Portuguese pernas is divided across the physical line break.
Nas completes pernas. Uchimata gooyaku begins a figurative example, compared with a plaster that adheres on both sides.

runs.text: que ſe pega dambas as partes: dizſe dos que

lines.note: The plaster sticks on both sides. The source applies this comparison to people, preparing the description of shifting allegiance below.

runs.text: ora ſão de hũa parte, ora de outra inconſtãtes.

lines.note: Those people are now on one side, now on the other, and are inconstant. This is the figurative explanation of uchimata gooyaku, not a literal medical instruction.
Uchimegui means breaking or undoing something. The principal form eida is retained as printed; the Portuguese desfa- continues below.
Zer completes desfazer, followed by algũa couſa. The line finishes the definition of breaking or dismantling an object.
Uchimomo is the inside of the thighs. The scan supports initial Vchi and the t in dentro, correcting OCR Vehimomo and denro.
Uchimono is identified as the polearm called Naguinata. The upright Japanese weapon name occurs within the Portuguese definition and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.
Uchimoraxi means letting someone escape. The last mark after eſca is a printed line-end hyphen, continuing escapar below, rather than the OCR's period.

runs.text: par alguem não o podendo matar, ou aleãçar.

lines.note: The person escapes because one cannot kill or reach him. The printed third letter in aleãçar looks e-like in this impression; that anomalous reading is retained provisionally rather than silently changed to expected alcançar.
Uchimucai describes being turned fully toward something. The carons in ǒ and ǒta are visible and retained in the principal forms.

runs.text: algũa parte, ou eſtar de fronte.

lines.note: The object may be a direction or part, with the alternative being face to face. This completes the orientation sense of uchimukai.
Uchimuqi similarly denotes turning toward a direction. The Portuguese virarſe corresponds to the reflexive motion, followed by an alternative state on the next row.
Ou eſtar de fronte adds being directly opposite or facing something. It completes the same entry rather than beginning another headword.
Uchimure is gathering in a group. The Portuguese first describes many people together, then narrows its usual application below.

runs.text: particularmẽte ſe diz de paßaros, ou animues.

lines.note: The expression is used particularly of birds or animals. The scan's vowel in animues is u-like, and the OCR-aligned form is retained with a caveat; animaes is the lexical interpretation, not an imposed transcription.
Uchinabicaxi means bending or causing something to incline. Its historical principal forms are retained; the physical example follows on the next row.

runs.text: como faz o vento às eruas, ou ramos. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Wind bending herbs or branches illustrates the literal sense. Itẽ introduces another use and preserves the abbreviation tilde rather than expanding it.
The additional sense is making people submit. Sono xei begins a cited Japanese example about the force or company, continued on the following row.

The cited phrase describes more than seven hundred mounted men of a province being brought to submission. Kokuchiu is represented by cocuchiǔ; the damaged long-u mark is retained as the provisional caron rather than replaced from a modern spelling.

runs.text: L. 36. Eſſa gente que era ſete-

lines.note: Taif. is the upright source label, followed by book 36 in the italic apparatus. The translation begins with the group numbering seven hundred or more; the visible hyphen in ſete- continues the number on the next row.

runs.text: centos, ou mais fazendo ſujeitar, & render

lines.note: Centos completes setecentos. The Portuguese continues the action of making that company submit and surrender, and the phrase carries over the page; the isolated a todos below is catchword furniture.
